messages.subject: Old style and new style classes
messages.subject_clean: Old style and new style classes
messages.body_plain:
I have been writing quick and dirty S-plus code for years, but for a recent 
project I took the plunge, bought Venables and Ripley's S Programming, and 
implemented a class library using new style classes (in S-Plus 6.0). It worked 
quite nicely and I am wondering about making more routine use of them. Before I 
make much more of an investment, I have a few questions, both factual and 
subjective, that I'd be grateful for opinions on. 

1) I don't use R at the moment, but I might, and might want to target users who 
do. The documentation at http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-lang.pdf seems 
to suggest that R 1.6.2 supports only old style classes, but 
http://developer.r-project.org/methodsPackage.html implies that new style 
classes can be used with the aid of a methods package from John Chambers. 
Venables and Ripley only describe old-style classes for R and add in their 
online supplement that there are 'small changes' between S-Plus and R for new 
style classes. Can the new style class mechanism be used in practice 
transparently and portably between S-Plus and R?

2) The s-news archives hold a few complaints about the design of the new style 
classes scattered over the last few years. On mature reflection, do people have 
opinions about the practical workability of old or new style classes for 
implementing reusable, object oriented code?

3) There are also some hints (eg top line of 
http://developer.r-project.org/classIssues.html) that new style classes have 
not been committed to by some active developers. Is this true? Do new style 
classes have an active future? Is R committed to them?   Insightful?   

I use old-style (S version3 engine) and new-style (S version4) classes in the 
sense of Venables and Ripley. 

 -------------------------------------
 Dr Jonathan Swinton
 Proteom Ltd 
 Babraham Hall
 Babraham
 Cambridge CB2 4AT
  www.proteom.com
 
 -----------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 1 Apr 2003, Jonathan Swinton wrote:

> I have been writing quick and dirty S-plus code for years, but for a
> recent project I took the plunge, bought Venables and Ripley's S
> Programming, and implemented a class library using new style classes (in
> S-Plus 6.0). It worked quite nicely and I am wondering about making more
> routine use of them. Before I make much more of an investment, I have a
> few questions, both factual and subjective, that I'd be grateful for
> opinions on.

> 1) I don't use R at the moment, but I might, and might want to target
> users who do. The documentation at
> http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-lang.pdf seems to suggest that R
> 1.6.2 supports only old style classes, but
> http://developer.r-project.org/methodsPackage.html implies that new
> style classes can be used with the aid of a methods package from John
> Chambers. Venables and Ripley only describe old-style classes for R and
> add in their online supplement that there are 'small changes' between 
> S-Plus and R for new style classes. Can the new style class mechanism be 
> used in practice transparently and portably between S-Plus and R?

R did not support S4 classes in 1999 when S Programming was written.
It does now, and as from version 1.7.0 (due April 16) it will support
them by default as the "methods" package will be loaded by default.

My experience is that those small differences have been a big disincentive
to portability.  There has recently been a big push to getting S4 classes
working well in R, but the details still catch me out a lot.
It is not clear that the R implementation is converging towards the S-PLUS 
6.x one, though.

> 2) The s-news archives hold a few complaints about the design of the
new style classes scattered over the last few years. On mature reflection, 
do people have opinions about the practical workability of old or new style 
classes for implementing reusable, object oriented code?

I think it is too early for `mature reflection': see my next answer.

> 3) There are also some hints (eg top line of 
http://developer.r-project.org/classIssues.html) that new style classes 
have not been committed to by some active developers. Is this true? 
Do new style classes have an active future? Is R committed to them?   
Insightful?

A very small proportion of active developers have been using them. Only
about 6 of the 206 packages on CRAN use them and 4 of those are variations
on the DBI theme.  There are very few third-party uses of S4 classes
available for S-PLUS 6.x.  (The BioConductor project uses S4 classes under
R, and there is an S-PLUS product based on that which I suppose does too.)

There is a lot more current interest in S4 classes in the R community: 
time will tell if this blossoms or dies off.

Until recently the desire to make code available for S-PLUS 2000 and R
was a major impediment to using S4 classes, but soon it will be reasonable 
to assume that most users have them available.

--

Jonathan,

I think you are asking the right questions.  SV4 has caused severe problems in 
S-Plus mainly due to lack of multiple inheritance.  I have been burned MANY 
times when running an object through a method (e.g., imputation) that sticks on 
an additional class.  Right now I am teaching a class using S-Plus 6 with my 
impute function in the Hmisc library and strange error messages are driving the 
students crazy.  So far all my tests in the R 1.7 development version indicate 
that R, unlike S-Plus, is backward compatible with old-style classes and 
methods.  But if you want to be compatible with S-Plus it would be nice if we 
could just avoid new classes and methods.  Unfortunately S-Plus does not let us 
do that either, because multiple old-style classes is not allowed any more.  

In the bigger picture,  I am still not really convinced that new classes and 
methods offer advantages to data analysts.  The new methods are not as flexible 
and take longer to program.  I frequently stick on a new element of a fit 
object list for debugging or for enhancing functions that others wrote.  You 
can't really do this with SV4.  Also, new methods and classes have made some 
code non-transportable across systems (primarily to older versions of S-Plus).  
There are now packages on CRAN that use slots to address elements while other 
versions of these same packages use list elements.  Hence some code retrieves 
details of fit objects using @ and some needs to use $.  I know that retrieving 
pieces of fit objects is inelegant (extractor methods should be written) but it 
is very common that I don't want to take the time to write an extractor method 
for every application, and I sure hate to waste time sensing whether the object 
was created using old vs. new style classes.

I know that new classes and methods are more elegant from a computer science 
perspective, but I analyze data and like to use what works (e.g., I really like 
both Perl and Python).  New methods provide much more safety.  I have found 
though that I don't need this kind of protection from myself.  I have plenty of 
other problems to worry about.

That's my $.02 worth.

-- 
Frank E Harrell Jr              Prof. of Biostatistics & Statistics
Div. of Biostatistics & Epidem. Dept. of Health Evaluation Sciences
U. Virginia School of Medicine  http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.subject: Improving efficiency in matching to the closest value
messages.subject_clean: Improving efficiency in matching to the closest value
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I have a vector of values jj which I want to match with another vector j, I
want to list all the values that are very close to jj and j, the following
will do the trick, but it can be very slow for large numbers like 10,000 for
example.

# set up a vector of reference values
j<-seq(0,1,length=1000)
# set up a vector of generated values.
jj<-runif(1000,0,1)

# calculate the absolute difference between the two.
jjj<-matrix(jj[rep(1:length(jj),length(j))],ncol=length(jj),byrow=T)
jjjj<-abs(matrix(j)[,rep(1,length(jj))]-jjj)

# give the output.
index<-apply(jjjj,2,function(x) which(x==min(x)))

# check:
plot(j[index],jj)

I wonder if there is a much more efficient way to get the same result? All
advice welcome :)

Steve.

****************************************************************************
**********

If you only wanted the closest or a sample from a distribution with 
probabilities that come from a distance function you can use the new 
whichClosest function in the latest Hmisc library.  Also take a look at the 
following code (not from Hmisc):

  whichClosest <- function(x, w) {
  ## x: vector of reference values
  ## w: vector of values to find closest matches in x
  ## Returns: subscripts in x corresponding to w
  i <- order(x)
  x <- x[i]
  n <- length(x)
  br <- c(-1e30, x[-n]+diff(x)/2,1e30)
  m <- length(w)
if(.SV4.) i[.C("S_binning3", x=as.double(w), m, as.double(br),
                 length(br), 0, 0, TRUE, TRUE)$x] else
  i[.C("S_binning2", x=as.double(w), m, as.double(br),
       length(br), 0, TRUE, TRUE)$x]
}
Define .SV4. as TRUE if running S-Plus 6, FALSE if not.
If you want more than one match, these won't help.
--

I'm running "S-PLUS 2000 Professional Edition Release 2 for Microsoft Windows" 
on Windows 2000 (Professional).  Recently I've been unable to save anything 
generated from within S-Plus.  After attempting to save I get the following 
error message:

Thanks,
Sally Rodriguez

Ellis, Spencer Graves and Joseph Lucke for their help. Using Jim Stapleton’s
notation, the matrix I am dealing with (of dimesion k by k) has the form 
a( I + cJ), 
where I is the k by k identity matrix and J is the k by k matrix of all ones.
Its inverse is (I - d J)/a, where
d = c/(1+13 c).

In my particular example, a=0.55636364, c= -0.083333339 and k=12 (not 13 as
stated before) and therefore d=1225490.279

Thank you again
Stefano

Well, sometimes a loop is OK, even in S-Plus.  You don't say which
version of S-Plus you are using, but I get the following results using
a loop (see below) to generate the index vector as above with:
Version 6.1.2 Release 2 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.6 : 2002
on a Sun Blade 1000 (750MHz CPU).

                CPU time (s)                    memory use (MB)
n       matrix/apply    vector/loop     matrix/apply    vector/loop
-----|---------------|---------------|---------------|-------------
  200     0.25            0.25            46              44 (minimum)
  500     0.84            0.71            52              44
 1000     2.52            1.67            75              44
 2000     9.52            4.51           174              44
 5000    51.8            19.9            815              45
 7500   157.2            45.8           1761              45
 8000   N/A              52.3           >2000             45
10000   N/A              72.7           >2000             45

Note the apply code exceeded 2GB memory with an "Unable to obtain
requested dynamic memory" error for n > 7500, but the loop code barely
exceeded the startup requirements.

# set up a vector of reference values
j <- seq(0, 1, length = n)
# set up a vector of generated values.
jj <- runif(n, 0, 1)

# set up the result vector
index <- numeric(n)

# calculate the minimum difference
for(i in 1:length(jj)) {
  jjj <- abs(j - jj[i])
  index[i] <- which(jjj == min(jjj))
}

Hope this helps,
Ray Brownrigg

Under R, that didn't seem to do what I interpreted the request to mean.

That probably indicates that I misinterpreted, but here is something that
does parts of what I thought he wanted, and might be of value to someone:

##############33
#First, make the array and correlation matrix:
 tst <- array(rnorm(100), dim=c(20, 5))
 ct <- cor(tst)
 diag(ct) <- 0
 ct[lower.tri(ct)] <- 0 #Get rid of pesky ties.
#This shows the n largest (in absolute value) correlations, where n=5.
 ct[order(abs(ct),decreasing=T)[1:5]]
#This shows their order in the matrix:
 order(abs(ct),decreasing=T)[1:5]
#to learn which they are, you need to apply a little arithmatic:
#R stores matrices in column-major order.  Therefore, to get the
#row and column numbers (and thus know what correlates to what):
 row <- order(abs(ct),decreasing=T)[1:5]%%d
 col <- order(abs(ct),decreasing=T)[1:5]%/%d +1
#It would be a REALLY bright idea to double-check the logic behind those.
###########

I'll leave it to anyone who's interested to put these in a function ... I'd
suggest something like

top.corrs <- function(matrix, n=1){put function here}

and it might also be a good idea to pretty up the returned object, maybe
using the row and column names, if any.

Hope this helps someone,
Nels

messages.subject: Pruning rules in regression trees, 0-SE vs. 1-SE
messages.subject_clean: Pruning rules in regression trees, 0-SE vs. 1-SE
messages.body_plain:
In MASS, 3rd edition, p. 312, Venables and Ripley state that, in pruning
a regression tree, ".....the complexity parameter may be chosen to
minimize xerror.  Am alternatvie procedure is to use the 1-SE rule, the
largest value with xerror within one standard deviation of the
minimum".

In their "Introduction to recursive partitioning using the RPART
routines", Atkinson and Therneau recommend the 1-SE rule.  

Similarly, in their "Recursive partitioning in the health sciences",
Zhang and Singer state "Empirical evidence suggests that the tree
selected with the 1-SE rule is more often than not superior to one
selected with the 0-SE rule (p. 40).

While I have the greatest respect for all the authors involved, none of
them give details of why the 1-SE rule is preferred, or when it is not
preferred, or what basis should be used for judging which to use.   Nor
do any give citations.  

The 0-SE rule has intuitive appeal, at least to me, since it is already
based on crossvalidation.  

Does anyone have details or thoughts on this?

Thanks

Peter

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am also puzzled by this 1-SE rule, especially since we 
don't know the relationship between this rule and the type I error. 

 

For a null dataset with lots of variables, this 1-SE rule might result in a 
type I error too high. In situtations where there are relatviely few variables, 
this rule might be too conservative. It is better to have a rule which is 
adaptive to the nature of the dataset (such as the dimention)

 

One possible thing to do is to use a "p-SE" rule, with p to 
be determined through a permutation procedure to satisfy the 
pre-specified type I error rate.

 

Kai Yu

messages.subject: Re: Question on generalized linear models
messages.body_plain:
Use of the Poisson error sets up a variance structure that is not 
appropriate for binomial data.  Here are three possibilities:

1. You have "extra-binomial" variation and need to set up a 2-stage model 
that accounts for variation that is not binomial.

2. You entered the percentages without entering the sample size, so the 
variance structure is not correct.

3. The regression function is not linear on the logistic scale.  In that 
case, fitting a more flexible curve such as a regression spline or low 
order polynomial might give a better fit.  This is the easiest of my 3 
possibilities to deal with, because a simple smooth of the (raw) data using 
loess or lowess will indicate pretty well if the regression function is 
sigmoid.  Alternatively, with the percentage data, you could plot the 
logit(percentage) with respect to your predictor, fit the least squares 
regression, and have a look at the residual.  These informal methods are 
crude, but I have found them to be very useful in determining an 
appropriate form for a parametric generalized model.

--Naomi Altman

messages.subject: top correlations
messages.body_plain:
Dear Colleagues:
Many thanks to Nick Ellis, Nels Tolmison, Chuck Taylor, Jean Adams and
Spencer Graves
for help on finding the cells in matrix containing top correlations.

The Chuck Taylor's solution works the best for me

function(X = matrix(data = rnorm(1000), 100, 5), N = 3)
{
        CM <- cor(X)
        rm <- row(CM)
        cm <- col(CM)
        ODmat <- CM
        ODmat[rm >= cm] <- 0
        ODcorrs <- as.vector(ODmat)
        top.N <- rev(sort(abs(ODcorrs)))[1:N]
        whi <- is.element(abs(ODmat), top.N)
        locs <- which(whi)
        cbind(rm[locs], cm[locs])
}  

Thanks again and have a good day
Simon

messages.subject: Re: Pruning rules in regression trees, 0-SE vs. 1-SE
messages.subject_clean: Pruning rules in regression trees, 0-SE vs. 1-SE
messages.body_plain:
Dear Peter,

CV is an estimate of the extra-sample prediction error.  If it is true
that "slight overfitting is not bad for prediction", then it makes sense
that in order to interpret the model it will be more appropriate to select
a "slightly smaller" model and this might also not hurt prediction.  

Also, for linear models AIC results in overfitting and since AIC
corresponds to GCV which in turn corresponds to leave-one-out CV this
is in line with the arguments above.

I don't know why 1 x SE is the limit to use.

For a chemometrics type prediction problem using ridge regression I
have compared the 0 x SE and the 1 x SE rules when using them to
select the ridge-parameter.  In my setup, on average the 0 x SE rule
is *better* with respect to prediction performance than the 1 x SE
rule.  However, the difference is non-significant except when
comparing the average difference in absolute values of the prediction
error.

If the purpose of the analysis is prediction I would go for the 0 x SE rule.

Regards,
Henrik

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

MASS3, pp.218-219, comments on the use of offset in GLMs. To explore the effect 
of the offset I build two models:

ax.1 <- glm(Postwt ~ Prewt + Treat + offset(Prewt),
            family = gaussian, data = anorexia)
ax.2 <- glm(Postwt ~ Prewt + Treat,
            family = gaussian, data = anorexia)

But there seems to be no effect:

> summary(ax.1, cor = F)$coef
                  Value Std. Error   t value 
(Intercept)  49.7711090 13.3909581  3.716770
      Prewt  -0.5655388  0.1611824 -3.508689
  TreatCont  -4.0970655  1.8934926 -2.163761
    TreatFT   4.5630627  2.1333359  2.138933

(Intercept)  49.7711090 13.3909581  3.716770

  TreatCont  -4.0970655  1.8934926 -2.163761
    TreatFT   4.5630627  2.1333359  2.138933

However, a different syntax gives slightly different results:
 
ax.3 <- glm(Postwt ~ Prewt + Treat, offset(Prewt),
            family = gaussian, data = anorexia)
> summary(ax.3, cor = F)$coef
                  Value Std. Error   t value 
(Intercept)  46.3855538 13.3671250  3.470122

  TreatCont  -4.3856822  1.8816679 -2.330742
    TreatFT   4.5616088  2.1098701  2.162033

As I understand it (after browsing on the list files), writting  ", 
offset(Prewt)," should be irrelevant since glm does not have offset as an 
argument. Then coefficients for ax.2 and ax.3 should be the same, but they are 
not.

Some hint of what is going on?

messages.subject: Re: objcopy - keeping the original time stamp?
messages.subject_clean: objcopy - keeping the original time stamp?
messages.body_plain:
> Is there an Splus command that copies objects by name but
> retains the original time stamp?

Pete,

I stumbled across your query and wondered if you'd had any reply.  I presume 
that the "time stamp" is the same as "Date" in Object Explorer.  If so, this is 
the time stamp from the OS, i.e. when the file in .Data\ was created.  To 
change the time stamp of the object amounts to changing the time stamp of the 
file.  You would need to manipulate the system clock to do this, which is not 
advisable on a routine basis!

The functions I write tend to return either a list or S4 object.  In this case, 
I include a component (or slot) when = date().  More generally, you can give 
every object a "when" attribute.  A (rather perverse?) way to do this is to 
define an assignment operator that does just that. 

"%<-%" <- function(x, value)
{
        n <- sys.parent()
        eval(substitute(x <- structure(value, when = date())), n)

}

> x %<-% 7
[1] 7
attr(, "when"):
[1] "Fri Apr 04 16:31:04 GDT 2003"

> y %<-% 9
[1] 9
attr(, "when"):
[1] "Fri Apr 04 16:31:19 GDT 2003"

> x + y
[1] 16
attr(, "when"):
[1] "Fri Apr 04 16:31:04 GDT 2003"

> ols1 %<-% lm((x %<-% runif(10)) ~ (y %<-% runif(10)))
Call:
lm(formula = (x %<-% runif(10)) ~ (y %<-% runif(10)))
...

> attr(ols1, "when")
[1] "Fri Apr 04 16:33:54 GDT 2003"

> attr(x, "when")
[1] "Fri Apr 04 16:33:54 GDT 2003"

This also seems to work with some replacements, including:

> attr(x, "when")
[1] "Fri Apr 04 16:33:54 GDT 2003"

> attr(x, "when") %<-% "Fri Apr 04 16:33:55 GDT 2003"
[1] "Fri Apr 04 16:33:55 GDT 2003"
attr(, "when"):
[1] "Fri Apr 04 16:40:52 GDT 2003"

Rgds,

Robert

messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I just want to summarize the response I got fot the
question I posted earlier regarding Semi Variance.

The question I posted was,

Any one know how to calculate semi-varaince using
splus.? And also any functions or scripts which might
be able to use to calculate min varince
portfolio...(actually minimum semi variance
portfolio.)

I got couple of response and I am summarizing it here.
Special thanks to Patrick Burns, David Jessop, Chris
Howden  for respondin and giving good thoughts.

David Jessop defined semi-variance as 
(1/n) SUM { (Min (0, x - t))^2 }
then coding this straight into S would be pretty good
(x [x < t] %*% x [x < t]) / length (x)
or
SUM (x [x < t] ^ 2) / length (x)
And MinVarince Optimization he suggested NUOPT.

Chris suggested AI-Geostatistics web page.

Patrick defined the semivariance of a single asset by
making any observation above the target as zeros and
calculating variance as usual. He also points that to
calculate co-semivarince it is tricker and he point
out to the method mentioned in the Risk Publications
book "Portfolio Construction and Risk Budgeting " by 
Bernd Scherer. Which in summary is just calculate the
correlation matrix as usual and then inflate it into a
variance matrix using the semi-variances.
For the optimization he suggest generic optimizors.

Thanks all for the response and comments.

JP

messages.subject: Summary: Error on save in S-Plus 2000 R2
messages.subject_clean: Summary: Error on save in S-Plus 2000 R2
messages.body_plain:
My problem was in the Windows permissions of the folders I was attempting to 
save to.  Because of a change to the group permissions script that runs when I 
log onto my company's network, I was suddenly not allowed to save from S-Plus 
to my regular file
locations.  The odd thing about this is that for most Windows application, I 
can save to any disk location I choose.  So, it had me stumped.  At this point 
I've determined that I can save to any folder in the S_PROJ location.  Still a 
pain, but worse to
have the IT people messing with my computer.

Thanks to all who responded!

Sally

If you experience a similar problem, you might want to check the following 
(excerpts from the responses I received):

1.  The only time I've ever encountered something like this is when either a 
workstation or O/S "user" setting or "permissions" setting had been changed or 
corrupted, such that I no longer had authorization to modify the directory by 
writing back to
_Data.  You might want to look at the security properties of the directory 
containing _Data (or _Prefs or whatever it is you can't modify) and see if you 
have permission to write to it.
2.  Check to see if your .prefs directory is corrupt (with S-Plus closed, 
delete .prefs folder then restart S-Plus
3.  Verify that you have sufficient memory to save the file.

Dear S-news friends...

The only response to me posting that I received is the following from
Robert Burbidge. (Thanks Robert!)  Robert's suggestion would provide
a neat solution, but at this time I don't want to add the additional
bookkeeping to the objects themselves.

Since posting my query I read Venables and Ripley's S Programming.
The windows version groups multiple objects in single database
files, so there is no simple way to carry along a date for each individually
on the OS level other than that assigned at the creation of the S object
database file.  Since objects in the two data directories are likely to be
grouped together in different files, there is no simple way to carry the
object creation date along with.

Pete

#    My posting:
###################################################
I use Splus 6.1 on XP.  I have written a routine that compares
file names and timestamps in identical directory structures on
my desktop and laptop.  object.summary provides the timestamp
info.  Of the paired objects in the two databases, I update whichever
is older to agree with the more recent using objcopy.

objcopy assigns the current time as the time stamp, rather than
copying the time stamp from the object being copied, which for
my purposes would be preferable.  (The next time I compare the
two directories, the routine concludes that the copy is newer
because of the time stamp and copies it back.  No errors result,
but it would be nice to retain the original time stamp.)

Is there an Splus command that copies objects by name but
retains the original time stamp?

The notes on the help page for objcopy say:

    "This function is unrelated to the copy function in the S-PLUS
    library section external."

but I have neither a library section named "external" nor any
documentation on a function "copy".

Thanks in advance,

Pete

###################################################

From: "Burbidge, Robert" <robert.burbidge at csfb.com>

> > Is there an Splus command that copies objects by name but
> > retains the original time stamp?
>
> Pete,
>
> I stumbled across your query and wondered if you'd had any reply.  I
presume that the "time stamp" is the same as "Date" in Object Explorer.  If
so, this is the time stamp from the OS, i.e. when the file in .Data\ was
created.  To change the time stamp of the object amounts to changing the
time stamp of the file.  You would need to manipulate the system clock to do
this, which is not advisable on a routine basis!
>
> The functions I write tend to return either a list or S4 object.  In this
case, I include a component (or slot) when = date().  More generally, you
can give every object a "when" attribute.  A (rather perverse?) way to do
this is to define an assignment operator that does just that.
>
> "%<-%" <- function(x, value)
> {
> n <- sys.parent()
> eval(substitute(x <- structure(value, when = date())), n)
>
> }
>
> > x %<-% 7
> [1] 7
> attr(, "when"):
> [1] "Fri Apr 04 16:31:04 GDT 2003"
>
> > y %<-% 9
> [1] 9
> attr(, "when"):
> [1] "Fri Apr 04 16:31:19 GDT 2003"
>
> > x + y

> > ols1 %<-% lm((x %<-% runif(10)) ~ (y %<-% runif(10)))

> lm(formula = (x %<-% runif(10)) ~ (y %<-% runif(10)))
> ...
>
> > attr(ols1, "when")
> [1] "Fri Apr 04 16:33:54 GDT 2003"
>
> > attr(x, "when")
> [1] "Fri Apr 04 16:33:54 GDT 2003"
>
> This also seems to work with some replacements, including:
>
> > attr(x, "when")
> [1] "Fri Apr 04 16:33:54 GDT 2003"
>
> > attr(x, "when") %<-% "Fri Apr 04 16:33:55 GDT 2003"
> [1] "Fri Apr 04 16:33:55 GDT 2003"
> attr(, "when"):
> [1] "Fri Apr 04 16:40:52 GDT 2003"
>
> Rgds,
>
> Robert

messages.subject: Re: Pruning rules in regression trees, 0-SE vs. 1-SE
messages.subject_clean: Pruning rules in regression trees, 0-SE vs. 1-SE
messages.body_plain:
The 1-SE rule was proposed and defended in Brieman, Friedman, Olshen and
Stone, Classification and Regression Trees, which is the foundational work
upon which tree and rpart were both built.  Get a copy of their book for
the full discussion.

  Consider a plot of x = model complexity (least to most) and y= error on some
scale.  There is a true curve, which falls to a minimum somewhere along this
x axis, and that is of course the model one wants.  In practice, the estimated
curve created by cross-validation often has a fairly wide "flat spot" for
it's minimum.  The 1-SE rule says in effect "all the models along this flat
lower area are essentially tied, so take the simplest one of the set".

  In simultations where the exact true model is one of the possible rpart
outputs, the cross-validated complexity curve can exhibit less of this
problem: the min is sharp, and the 1-SE rule oversmooths.  I think that 
simulations like the Brieman et al waveform data, where the exact truth is
NOT one of the possible rpart solutions, are more realistic.  After all, that
is the world in which I will actually apply the model.  But the art of
well designed simulations is just that --- an art.  And properly integrating
and interpreting the full spectrum of results from the many se-rule simulations
is even harder...

  Only an opinion.  

        Terry Therneau

messages.body_plain:
KDD Cup 2003  (http://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/kddcup/index.html)
------------

 The Ninth ACM SIGKDD International Conference on 
 Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2003)
 

Every year, in conjunction with the ACM SIGKDD conference, a knowledge
discovery and data mining competition (KDD Cup) is held to challenge 
the research community in industry and academia.

This year's competition focuses on problems motivated by network
mining and the analysis of usage logs. Complex networks have emerged
as a central theme in data mining applications, appearing in domains
that range from communication networks and the Web, to biological
interaction networks, to social networks and homeland security.
At the same time, the difficulty in obtaining complete and accurate
representations of large networks has been an obstacle to research in
this area. 

This KDD Cup is based on a very large archive of research papers that
provides an unusually comprehensive snapshot of a particular social
network in action; in addition to the full text of research papers, it
includes both explicit citation structure and (partial) data on the
downloading of papers by users. It provides a framework for testing
general network and usage mining techniques, which will be explored
via four varied and interesting task. Each task is a separate
competition with its own specific goals.

To learn more about the KDD cup competition rules, the tasks, and the
datasets, please visit the KDD cup web site managed by 
the KDD cup chairs Johannes Gehrke, Paul Ginsparg and Jon Kleinberg. 

For more information, please refer to the SIGKDD Conference web site

http://www.acm.org/sigkdd/kdd2003/

or go directly to the KDD Cup 2003 web site

http://www.cs.cornell.edu/projects/kddcup/index.html

                          Call for Papers

                     The Fifth WEBKDD Workshop: 
Web Mining as a Premise to Effective and Intelligent Web Applications

                   http://db.cs.ualberta.ca/webkdd03/

                   Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
                August 24-27, 2003 - Washington, DC, USA

Important Dates
---------------
Abstracts due: Tuesday May 27th, 2003
Papers due:    Tuesday June 3rd, 2003 
Notification:  Friday June 27th, 2003
Camera Ready:  Thursday July 17th, 2003

WEBKDD'03 is the 5th of a successful series of workshops on knowledge
discovery in the Web. The Web presents a key driving force for a large
spectrum of applications, in which a user or even an application can
interact with a company, a governmental authority, a non-governmental
organization or a non-profit institution. To develop effective and
intelligent web-applications and web services, it is essential to
analyse patterns hidden in the usage of web resources, their contents
and their interconnections. User preferences and expectations together
with usage patterns form the basis for personalized, user-friendly and
business-optimal services. Contents, and link structures as well as
the semantic web are paramount for the development of good wrappers
for intelligent web agents. Enabling technologies include data mining,
document analysis and classification, user modelling and quality
evaluation models for them.  
The WEBKDD'03 workshop aims at bringing together practitioners on
web-commerce, portals and ASPs, decision-makers in
[MSOffice1]non-commercial institutions that exploit web technologies
to optimize their services, technology providers, and data mining
researchers to foster the exchange of ideas and the dissemination of
emerging solutions on user and usage modelling for effective and
intelligent web-based applications using web usage, structure and
content mining.   

Workshop Co-Chairs:
-------------------
* Ronny Kohavi (Blue Martini Software, USA)
* Bing Liu (University of Illinois at Chicago, USA)
* Brij Masand (Data Miners Inc., USA)
* Jaideep Srivastava (University of Minnesota, USA)
* Osmar R. Zaïane (University of Alberta, Canada)

For inquiry, send e-mail to
 webkdd03 at cs.ualberta.ca

Topics of interest:
------------------- 
WEBKDD '03 calls for contributions related to data mining of web log
data, site information, document contents, user records and
preferences; the exploitation of the mining results for user
profiling, user modeling, web structure and content mining, and web
usage metrics and intelligent web applications. These include the
following subjects: 

-Web Usage based Business Metrics 
* Relationship of appropriate web usage data capture and
  pre-processing methods to business metrics 
* Reliability and consistency of Metrics
* Integration of click stream data with back end data and related metrics
* Intelligent summarization/explanation of changes in key web usage metrics.

-Enabling technologies: (limitations and strengths)
* Data warehousing (both web and non-web data)
* Data collection including event streams, such as click streams, call
  center streams, and transactional data
* Techniques for web data preparation, including cleansing,
  transformation, and sampling
* Classification of web page texts and multimedia content

-Modeling users and usage:
* Profile establishment upon declared and derived preferences
* Deriving profiles from usage
* Discovering misuse and fraud
* Recommendation systems
* Student profiles in e-learning
* Alert systems
* Permission marketing

-Web content and structure mining:
* Wrapper generation and information extraction
* Web content and/or structure mining
* Semantic Web mining
* Web mining for business intelligence and for security

-Applications:
* Recommendation systems, such as travel assistants
* E-learning, such as collectors of personalized teaching materials
* Alert systems, such as personalized delivery of news and journals
* Fraud and misuse detection, such as credit-card fraud and network
  intrusion detection 
* Web log (and other types of log) analysis for security applications

Publication of the workshop proceedings:
----------------------------------------
The workshop notes will be published by ACM and distributed during the
workshop.  

The full version of the accepted papers will be published by
Springer-Verlag after a second round of reviews pending
approval. Springer has published the proceedings of WEBKDD 1999, 2001,

sum(abs(outer(V, V, "-"))) is the most obvious way, and will be fast

messages.subject: Re: For posting to S-News [aggregate absolute difference]
messages.subject_clean: For posting to S-News [aggregate absolute difference]
messages.body_plain:
> We need a fast algorithm to calculate the aggregate difference between
> all members of a numeric vector:
> For a vector V, with n elements Ei, x=sum(abs((Ei-Ej)) for all ij
> combinations of elements in the vector.
> Thanks,
> Christophe Benoist 

If the vector is long enough that N^2 is more memory than you want to use,
but short enough to be sorted, then I think the following should work.
(You could put this on all line but I've broken out the computation for
legibility.)  Note that this gives half the value of Brian's solution
due to ignoring order; double if you wish.

sumdiff <- function(x)
{       ## sum of absolute differences of pairs (counting each pair once
        ## regardless of order)
d <- diff(sort(x))
N1 <- length(d)
sum((1:N1)*(N1:1)*d)
}

The idea is that once you sort, each difference between values is the sum
of the consecutive differences along the way.  So each difference of 
consecutive values appears a number of times equal to the number of values
to the left times the number of values to the right.

        Alan Zaslavsky
        zaslavsk at hcp.med.harvard.edu

messages.subject: Re: Summary of Meaning of Intercept Term in Regression
messages.subject_clean: Summary of Meaning of Intercept Term in Regression
messages.body_plain:
Thanks very much fro the responses I got from Spencer Graves, Naomi Altman and Samuel Buttrey. Listed below is the responses I got followed by the question.

>From Spencer Graves:

If you center all potentially explanatory variables to mean 0, then the 

intercept is the mean.  Otherwise, it moves about as the slope changes, 

as is obvious if you make a plot.

>From Naomi Altman:

You are correct that the intercept is affected by other predictors and is not the mean of response. It is simply the predicted value of the response when all the other predictors are zero.

>From Samuel Buttrey:

Spencer is right. What you said is also right: the intercept is the estimated value of Y when all the X's are 0. (For categorical predictors, replace "are 0" with "are at their baseline values.") In many cases, the intercept has no real meaning as a quantity. For example, if you're modeling "number of months served" as a function of age, gender, race, and IQ, the intercept measures the expected number of months for people with age = 0, gender and race at the baseline, and IQ = 0. This is not very useful!

My original question:

> Hi, S+ users, if understand correctly the QR decomposition for 

> estimating parameters in linear regression, the intercept term is 

> affected by other predictor variables. So hard to figure it out what 

> that intercept term really means. I think that is not telling the 

> overall mean of response variable unless effects of predictors are zero. 

> Can somebody shed light on this subject? I really appreciate for your help.

> 

>

messages.subject: Re: fit linear combination of normal and beta
messages.subject_clean: fit linear combination of normal and beta
messages.body_plain:
We can write a likelihood and apply maximum likelihood, as follows:

   f(Y | var.x, A, shape1, shape2)
    = integral{
        dnorm(y-A*E, mean=0, sd=sqrt(var.x)) *
          dbeta(E, shape1, shape2)*dE }

We can write a function to evaluate this integral using a simple 
numerical integration (sum of a product of vectors).  Then give to 
"optim" in the MASS library to estimate (log(var.x), A, log(shape1), 
log(shape2)).

	  Estimation in terms of log(var.x), log(shape1) and log(shape2), 
rather than var.x, shape1, and shape2, avoids problems with illegal 
negative values.  In addition, when I've made contour plots of crudely 
similar log(likelihoods) vs. parameters two at a time, I've found that 
the log(likelihood) surface was more nearly normal in the transformed 
space than in the original space with the finite boundaries.  This means 
that the normal approximation to the distribution of the maximum 
likelihood estimates works better in the transformed space.  Confidence 
intervals can be computed in the transformed space and then 
back-transformed.

Hope this helps.
Spencer Graves

messages.subject: Re: cusumtest critical values
messages.body_plain:
There are better tests than the CUSUM for testing structural stability of
coefficients. Notable tests are the LM test of Nyblom (1989) JASA and the
extensions by Bruce Hansen (Journal of Policy Modeling 1992). I have S code
to compute the Nyblom and Hansen tests using the output of the FinMetrics
function OLS. These functions may be easily modified to work with the output
of the function lm. For example, here is code to compute the Hansen tests

HansenTest =
##
## This function implements Hansen's tests for parameter constancy over time
in the
## linear regression model.
##
## Input an "OLS" object returned from the FinMetrics function OLS
##
## Reference: Hansen, B. (1992). "Testing for Parameter Instability in
Linear Models,"
## Journal of Policy Modeling, 14, 517-533.
##
function(object) {
        resid = residuals(object)
        if (is(resid, "timeSeries")) {
                resid = seriesData(resid)
        }
        call = object$call
        var.names = names(object$coef)
        test.names = c(var.names,"sigma^2")
        x = model.matrix(object)
        n = length(resid)
        sigma2 = sum(resid^2)/n
        fi = (x * as.vector(resid))[n:1, , drop=F]
        fi = cbind(fi,(resid^2 - sigma2)[n:1])
        si = colCumsums(fi)
        vi = colSums(fi^2)
        V.inv = solve(crossprod(fi))
        li.stats = colSums(si^2)/(n*vi)
        names(li.stats) = test.names
        lc.stat = sum(diag(V.inv %*% crossprod(si)))/n
        ans = list(li.stats=li.stats,
                            lc.stat=lc.stat,
                                 call=call)
        oldClass(ans) = "HansenTest"
        ans
}

"print.HansenTest" =
function(x, digits=4, ...)
{
        coef.stat = x$li.stats
        joint.stat = format(round(x$lc.stat,digits=digits))

        q = length(coef.stat)
        kVec = 1:20
        qMat = matrix(c(0.353, 0.470, 0.748,
                   0.610, 0.749, 1.07,
                   0.846, 1.01, 1.35,
                   1.07,  1.24, 1.60,
                   1.28,  1.47, 1.88,
                   1.49,  1.68, 2.12,
                                          1.69,  1.90, 2.35,
                                          1.89,  2.11, 2.59,
                                          2.10,  2.32, 2.82,
                                          2.29,  2.54, 3.05,
                                          2.49,  2.75, 3.27,
                                          2.69,  2.96, 3.51,
                                          2.89,  3.15, 3.69,
                                          3.08,  3.34, 3.90,
                                          3.26,  3.54, 4.07,
                                          3.46,  3.75, 4.30,
                                          3.64,  3.95, 4.51,
                                          3.83,  4.14, 4.73,
                                          4.03,  4.33, 4.92,
                   4.22,  4.52, 5.13), byrow=T, ncol=3)
        colIds(qMat) = c("10%","5%","1%")
        cat("\nTest for Constancy of Regression Parameters: Hansen Tests\n\n")
        cat("Null Hypothesis: constant parameters\n")
        cat("\nCall:\n")
        dput(x$call)
        cat("\nIndividual Coefficient Test Statistics:\n")
        print(signif(coef.stat, digits=digits))
        cat("\nCritical Values:\n")
        print(qMat[1,])
        cat("\nJoint Test Statistic: ")
        cat(joint.stat, "\n")
        if (q < 20) {
                cat("\nCritical Values:\n")
                print(qMat[q,])
        }
        invisible()
}

messages.body_plain:
> > Hi,
>
> Is there any way to ascertain if there is structural instability in
> a time series regression model without having to visually inspect
> the graphs of the cusum statistics from the recursive least squares
> estimation.
>
> Can someone let me have the formula or routine as to how to compute
> the critical bands for the cusum statistic.

The p values for the Recursive CUSUM test can be derived from crossing 
probabilities of a Brownian motion, the respective formula is 
essentially given in the first formula on page 154 of the original 
Brown, Durbin, Evans (1975) paper in JRSS.

For R there is a package called "strucchange" on CRAN at
  http://CRAN.R-project.org/
which contains the Recursive and the OLS CUSUM and MOSUM test as well 
as estimates-based fluctuation tests and the supF, aveF and expF test, 
already with hard-wired p value functions (possibly derived from 
simulated tables of critical values).

Likelihood-based flucutation processes including the Nyblom test which 
Eric Zivot mentioned are not (yet) available in strucchange, but will 
be in the next version (hopefully in a few months).

Best,
Achim

> Best Regards
> Arjun Bhandari

messages.subject: Re: Calculating Percentiles
messages.body_plain:
Dear Padma,

At 11:34 AM 4/9/2003 -0700, Padma Illindra wrote:

> Can any of you help me with calculating percentiles using S-plus.
>
>
>
> I have a vector of values:
>
>
>
> vect <- c(20,60,30,69,21)
> I need to get the percentile value of each of these values among rest of the
> values. So, the function should retrun me same number of values saying what
> is the percentile value of 20 among all of the values? Similarly what is the
> percentile value of 60,30,69,21 among all of the values.
> Is there any function in S-plus to do this?
> Thanks in advance ofr the help.
> Padma

If I understand correctly what you want, and supposing that data contains 
the data vector, then the following should do the trick:

        100*colSums(outer(data, vect, "<"))/length(data)

I hope this helps,
 John

messages.subject: Re: Calculating Percentiles
messages.body_plain:
Two little postscripts on these solutions.

1. the original example used integers which suggests to me that ties might
be an issue.  You can easily modify either solution to make a simple
adjustment for ties, for example

        fn <- function(x, y) (x < y) + (x == y)/2
        colMeans(outer(data, vect, fn)) * 100

2. Andy's solution may not work inside a function if data and vect are both
local variables.  Fixing things so that it does work inside a function in
S-PLUS is an easy exercise.  (There is another system 'not unlike' S-PLUS
with different scoping rules where it will work, but I digress...)

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: multiphase regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus users:

I would like to know whether there have been libraries of SPLUS  suitable
for "multiphase regression." I just realized that this method may be useful
for my purpose, therefore, I am still accumulating basic knowledge on it.
If you kindly let me know some relevant pointers (e.g., books, book
chapter), they are also very welcomed.

Thanks in advance.

-Tadashi

PS:  Here's simplified sketch of what I wish to do:

Suppose we measure the temperature of the material by every 1 min.  First 5
min, we do not heat it.  During this period, we would like to know steady
state of the temperature.  Then after this 5 min. duration, we start heating
it for 5 min and stop it.  I would like to estimate a kind of index which
(may) corresponds to "when" the temperature of the material gets higher than
the original temperature measured for first 5 min.

I assume that I need one regression for steady state (first 5 min) and one
regression for rising phase of the temperature.  I may need another
regression for decaying phase.  This might be corresponding to "multiphase
regression" as far as I can understand.  If not, please correct me.

messages.subject: SUMMARY: Strange behaviour of offset
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Charles Anderson, Sam Buttrey and Brian Ripley for their 
comments to a message I posted a week ago (I am summarizing as soon as I have 
come back from field work). C.Anderson and B.Ripley detected that Prewt 
coefficients for ax.1 
(-0.57) and ax.2 (0.43) were different (see below the original message). 
Indeed, as C.Anderson pointed out: "There is no coefficient fit for the offset 
term; it is added into the linear predictor.", and this lead to the Prewt 
coefficient for ax.2 being 0.43-1. But what about the difference between 
coefficients for ax.2 and ax.3? S.Buttrey noticed that "offset(Prewt)"  
produces a vector that glm takes as an unnamed argument. The first argument in 
glm that I did not named is "weights", so ax.3 was really doing a weighted 
regression with Prewt as the weights. This can be seen with:

> ax.3 <- glm(Postwt ~ Prewt + Treat, offset(Prewt), family = gaussian, 
 data = anorexia)
> ax.4 <- glm(Postwt ~ Prewt + Treat, weights = Prewt, family = gaussian, 
 data = anorexia)

messages.subject: .wmf plots
messages.body_plain:
Daer S-users,

I have a delicate problem that occupies my mind the last two days. I
wrote a simply script that reads the .xls file names, imports the
desired columns, makes four plots and saves each page as a .wmf graphic.

Here is the end part of it:

#........ # data reading, transforming, etc functions

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
        plot.timeSeries(Ylogret)
        plot.timeSeries(Y)
        hist(Ylogret@data,nclass=50,prob=T,xlab=Ylogret@title)
        qqnorm(Ylogret@data,ylab=Ylogret@title)   
        qqline(Ylogret@data,type="l")

export.graph(FileName=OutputName,Name="GSD2",ExportType="EMF")

This gave me 25 wmf pictures with four plots each. After inserting these
pictures into Word everything looked fine. Each .wmf picture takes about
a half A4 page in Word and the size of the plots is readably. Finally
I've decided to add another two plots;

par(mfrow=c(3,2))
        plot.timeSeries(Ylogret)
        plot.timeSeries(Y)
        hist(Ylogret@data,nclass=50,prob=T,xlab=Ylogret@title,col=2)
        qqnorm(Ylogret@data,ylab=Ylogret@title)   
        qqline(Ylogret@data,type="l")
        meplot(abs(Ylogret@data[Ylogret@data<0]))
        hill(Ylogret@data,end=600)

Now, the size of the inserted pictures is still the same no matter how
many plots I generate (about half of an A4 page). This does not look
nice. I would like to have the same size of each plot but instead of
four now six.
Following some advices in books and help pages I've made some attempts
with adjusting the size of 'graphsheet()'. It helped to make the picture
bigger in Splus but not in Word. Only the JPG and PNG format preserved
the desired size but with very low quality.
After a sleepless night I've found the 'win.graph()' function. Adjusting
the width to 9 and height to 11 and inserting it into Word gives me the
desired size.
However, the characteristics of each plot are lost. The colours are
different, the lines are thicker. By trial and error using the
'pointsize', 'line.colors' and 'line.width.factor' arguments I've
managed to restore some of the characteristics but far from all.
Especially the Hillplot looks unattractive. Originally, the confidence
interval is dotted blue and the estimation is a line black. Now I have
all in lines and in colours that not match with histogram or the
reference grid in plot.timeSeries.

Now I have a problem, either nice plots but very small or large plots
but not good-looking.

Are they any solutions to keep the original plot characteristics in
win.graph()?

Or, how to keep the size of graphsheet() to be the same in Word? 

Thank you in advance.

G.D.

Splus 6 Release 2
Word 2002
Windows XP pro

Thanks to all. I have solved the problem. It was simpler than expected.
Just type 'graphsheet(orientation="portrait")'. It is not even necessary
to define the height and width.

Okay, I think I understand better now.  How about something like this
...

graphsheet(width = 8.5, height = 11)      # or whatever the measurements

par(mfrow=c(4, 2))

This sets up space for *eight* plots on a portrait-oriented page.  You
can
use this approach for both sets of graphs.  You will fill up just the

messages.subject: Models for survival data with heavy censoring
messages.subject_clean: Models for survival data with heavy censoring
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a problem analogous to this situation --
I visit an island for a week. I find out how old
is each person; they're all less than 100 years old.
Nobody dies while I'm there. When I leave, I think 
to myself, "Well, I guess these people are immortal,"
because I didn't see anyone die.

>From what I can tell, censored data will bias
the predicted survival distribution toward longer
survival times. I am working with perhaps 50% to
90% censored data, so the bias seems enough to
be a bother.

The one thing I can think of is to assume that
the population has reached a steady state, so
that something can be extracted from the 
distribution of current ages. I believe that
this approach will yield a penalty term for the
usual log likelihood function.

Any comments or references you may have are 
appreciated very much. I have checked some 
standard references, but I was unable to find
a discussion of this topic.

Regards,

Robert Dodier

messages.body_plain:
Hello, nlme-experts among the list members,

I would like to change the behavior of the function plot.aufPred() from
the nlme-library, version 3.3.1 (using S-PLUS, Ver. 6.0 Rel. 1 for Sun
SPARC, SunOS 5.6): I want to change the panel order of the trellis plot of
an augPred object.

To give an example: I have a multiply-nested (actually only doubly-nested)
groupedData object:

> A.gD <- groupedData( Y ~ X | ID/Vessel, data= A.df,
+               order.groups= list( ID= F, Vessel= T)

Y and X are of class numeric. ID and Vessel are of class factor, and
Vessel is actually nested within ID. (Note the groups-ordering according
to Vessel within each level of ID!)

Here is an extract from A.gD and some information on the levels of ID and
Vessel:

> A.gD
Grouped Data: Y ~ X | ID/Vessel
          ID  Y     X Vessel
   1   0-9-D  0 0.000      1
....
  10   0-9-D  3 3.000      1
  11   0-9-D  1 0.000      2
....
  20   0-9-D  2 3.000      2
.... .... ....
1321 PLV-5-D  0 0.000    133
....
1330 PLV-5-D  2 3.000    133
1331 PLV-5-D  0 0.000    134
....
1340 PLV-5-D 17 3.000    134

> levels( X$ID)
[1] "0-11-D"  "0-14-D" .... "CEN-4-D" "CEN-5-D"

> levels( X$Vessel)
[1] "1"   "2"   "3" .... "133" "134"

Issuing

> plot( A.gD)

gives a trellis plot with one panel of Y versus X for each level of
Vessel. The order of these "Vessel-panels" is (of course) as follows:

Panels belonging to the same ID-level are plotted adjacent to each other,
forming "ID-groups" of Vessel-panels. These ID-groups are arranged
according to the ordering of the ID-levels.
Within each ID-group the order of the Vessel-panels is determined (by
dafault) by the maximum value of Y within each Vessel-level.

Now, fitting a lme-model, producing the augmented predictions and plotting
them

> A.lme <- lme( Y ~ X, random= ~ X | ID/Vessel, data= A.gD)
> A.aP <- augPred( A.lme, length.out= 2)
> plot( A.aP)

gives also a trellis plot with one panel for each level of Vessel
(displaying the respective fitted model), but in the order of the
Vessel-levels and disregarding the ordering of the ID-levels.

Does anybody know an easy way to "extract" the panel order of the plot of
the groupedData object A.gD and to "transfer" it to the plot of the
augPred object A.aP?

Thank you for any sugestions! I will summarize to the list.

 Best regards  --  Gerrit

International Call for Contributed Papers *** and Registration ***
         Santa Cruz Bayesian data analysis workshop, 7-10 Aug 2003

Greetings, and apologies for cross-posting.

I wrote a few weeks ago to provide some details on the 

            International Workshop on Bayesian Data Analysis

which will take place on the campus of the University of California, Santa
Cruz (UCSC), from Thursday (evening) through Sunday (afternoon) 7-10 Aug
2003, as a kind of satellite meeting to be held right after the Joint
Statistical Meetings (JSM) nearby in San Francisco, CA, from August 3-7,
2003.

This message is to say that 

--> formal registration for the meeting is now open, and substantial
    travel funds are available to help with the costs associated with 
    participating in the workshop (since it's a satellite meeting to the
    JSM, we're hoping that most participants can cover their airfares
    to and from San Francisco; beyond that we expect to be able to offer
    partial or full support, to help defray local expenses, to a
    substantial number of contributed-paper participants).

If you'd like to participate in the meeting, please go to the conference
web page 

  www.ams.ucsc.edu/bayes03

and click on the relevant links -- you can (1) register and (2) submit the
abstract for your contributed paper, and you can also examine (3) the
overview of the workshop, (4) the list of invited participants and the
topics of their talks, (5) the summary of the deadlines, (6) a description
of Santa Cruz and UCSC, (7) a description of the arrangements for lodging
and meals, and (8) a summary of your transportation options.

If you have questions about the workshop that this message and/or the web
site do not answer, please send an email message to

  workshop at ams.ucsc.edu

The Organizing Committee for the Workshop is the Statistics Group in the
Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics (AMS) at UCSC, 

  David Draper <draper at ams.ucsc.edu> (Chair, AMS)
  Thanasis Kottas <thanos at ams.ucsc.edu>
  Herbie Lee <herbie at ams.ucsc.edu>
  Raquel Prado <raquel at ams.ucsc.edu>
  Bruno Sanso (Chair, Organizing Committee) <bruno at ams.ucsc.edu>

, and someone from this committee will read your message and respond to it 
quickly.

The meeting is sponsored by AMS, the Intelligent Systems and RIACS groups
at NASA Ames, the National Science Foundation, the Center for Biomolecular
Science and Engineering and the California Institute for Quantitative
Biomedical Research at UCSC, and the Research Department at
CTB/McGraw-Hill.  

If you're interested in giving a contributed paper at this Workshop in a
Valencia-style poster session, or if you're just interested in attending,
we would welcome your participation.

Attendance will be capped at about 100-120 people, and at present about 55
of these slots are taken, so there is plenty of room at the moment to join
the Workshop -- if you were already planning to come to the JSM in San
Francisco and you'd like to extend your stay in the Bay Area by a few days
(or if you'd just like to come to Santa Cruz), to hear some outstanding
talks and poster presentations on contemporary Bayesian data analysis in a
beautiful setting (the UCSC campus is located in a 2,000 acre redwood
forest overlooking Monterey Bay), please join us.

A more extended description of the Workshop follows.

Best wishes, and looking forward to seeing you in Santa Cruz, David Draper

                       Description of the Workshop

The focus of the Workshop will be Bayesian data analysis: starting with a
real problem in science or decision-making, formulating the problem in
statistical terms, using Bayesian methods to solve the original problem,
and discussing the strengths and weaknesses of the solution both
statistically and substantively, with plenty of attention to the interplay
between the real-world context and the Bayesian model-building, checking,
and reformulating.

The meeting will be held on the campus of the University of California,
Santa Cruz (UCSC), immediately after the Joint Statistical Meetings that
will take place from August 3-7 in nearby San Francisco.  

The goal is to bring together 100-120 people interested in Bayesian
applications in a variety of disciplines, including (but not limited to)
bioinformatics, biostatistics, econometrics, engineering, epidemiology,
computer science, machine learning, and statistics.  

We hope that the setting of the UCSC campus, in a beautiful grove of
redwood trees overlooking Monterey Bay, will create a fruitful atmosphere
for multidisciplinary discussions and transfer of ideas.

We expect invited sessions on at least the following topics:

  * Bioinformatics
  * Biostatistics/epidemiology
  * Computation
  * Engineering applications
  * Machine learning/computer science
  * Nonparametric and semiparametric methods
  * Spatiotemporal modeling

The workshop is scheduled for 7-10 August 2003. 

The organization of the meeting will be as follows: 

* Participants will be encouraged to arrive on the evening of Thu 7 Aug to
  register and take part in an opening mixer;

* There will be four invited sessions on Fri 8 Aug;

* Contributed papers will be presented in a Valencia-style poster session
  in the evening of Fri 8 Aug;

* There will be four invited sessions on Sat 9 Aug;

* The conference banquet will take place in the evening of Sat 9 Aug;
  and

* There will be an optional conference excursion to a winery in the Santa
  Cruz mountains on Sun 10 Aug.

The workshop is intended for statisticians, scientists and engineers (from
a wide variety of fields of specialization) involved in applications
requiring statistical inference, prediction, and decision-making and using
Bayesian methods.

The costs of participation in the Workshop are as follows:

* The meeting will be residential on the UCSC campus, with most 
  participants staying in apartments located within walking distance of 
  the conference venue (you're of course free to stay off-campus if you 
  wish); the approximate daily cost of room and board on-campus is
  $100, and we encourage participants to arrive on Thu afternoon and 
  depart on Sun afternoon.

* The registration fee, which will cover the rental of the rooms where the
  talks and poster session will be held, the audiovisual equipment, and
  other global workshop expenses, is $75.

* We will organize one or more buses to take participants from the JSM to
  Santa Cruz on Thu afternoon (this will be included in the registration
  fee); if you prefer to organize your own transport, the approximate cost 
  from San Francisco or the San Francisco airport is $50 each way.

* The (optional) conference banquet on Sat night will cost $30; the cost
  of the (optional) winery excursion on Sun has not yet been determined.

Financial support is available (as described above) and should be
requested at time of registration (we expect to provide partial support to
a substantial number of participants who are making contributed
presentations).

The (initial) registration deadline for the Workshop is 9 June? 2003.

As long as places are still available, registration will continue after
this date up to and including the first day of the meeting, but after 9
June it may be more difficult for you to (a) have your contributed paper
listed in the program and (b) receive full consideration for funding
support. 

Participation in the workshop will be limited, and consideration will be
given to program balance.

Special consideration will be given to young investigators and Ph.D. 
students, and members of under-represented groups are especially
encouraged to apply.

By virtue of (a) its spectacular setting, nestled within 2,000 acres of
redwood forest and meadows overlooking the Monterey Bay National Marine

the University of California, Santa Cruz is considered one of the most

It's located about 70 miles (115 km) south of San Francisco and 30 miles

Santa Cruz itself (population around 50,000) is a beach resort close to

The weather in the summer usually features bright but mild sunny days with

messages.subject: Summary: multiphase regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus users:

I received one suggestion from Dr. Nielsen which is quite helpful.

------starts here-----
I am not familiar with the term "multiphase regression", but based on your
description I think the most simple solution would be a linear spline,
i.e. something like:

lm(Temp ~ -1 + bs(tt, Boundary.knots = c(0, 30), knots=seq(5,30,by=1),
                  intercept = T, deg = 1), data = "whatever"))

This fits a strait line between 0 and 5 minutes and thereafter a curve by
pasting lines of length 1 minute together - the whole curve will be
contineous ( data must contain the temperature (Temp) and time (tt), it
is assumed that max(tt) is 30 and that you sample several times per minute).

You will also be able to use more advanced B-spline bases where  the
information regarding the time interval of heating is used (constant for 5
minutes and only contineous at 10 minutes).  

If you measure / know  the heat input and make some appropriate
assumptions about the heat transfer I think you will be able to derive a
non-linear regression model.

------ ends here -------

I did not know quite well the term "multiphase regression."  A book,
"Nonlinear regression" by G.A.F. Seber and C.J. Wild (John Wiley & Sons
Inc.), Chapter 9, "multiphase and spline regression" describes the
theoretical basis of this regression.

The following is my original posts.  Anyone who gives me further suggestion
is very much appreciated.

Thank you very much.

-Tadashi

----original post----
I would like to know whether there have been libraries of SPLUS  suitable
for "multiphase regression." I just realized that this method may be useful
for my purpose, therefore, I am still accumulating basic knowledge on it.
If you kindly let me know some relevant pointers (e.g., books, book
chapter), they are also very welcomed.

Thanks in advance.

-Tadashi

PS:  Here's simplified sketch of what I wish to do:

Suppose we measure the temperature of the material by every 1 min.  First 5
min, we do not heat it.  During this period, we would like to know steady
state of the temperature.  Then after this 5 min. duration, we start heating
it for 5 min and stop it.  I would like to estimate a kind of index which
(may) corresponds to "when" the temperature of the material gets higher than
the original temperature measured for first 5 min.

I assume that I need one regression for steady state (first 5 min) and one
regression for rising phase of the temperature.  I may need another
regression for decaying phase.  This might be corresponding to "multiphase
regression" as far as I can understand.  If not, please correct me.

Subject: SIGKDD Data Mining Innovation and Service Awards : Nominations sought

http://www.kdnuggets.com/news/2003/n07/1i.html

ACM SIGKDD, the leading data mining society, invites your nominations for
1. SIGKDD Innovation Award, and 
2. SIGKDD Service Award.

SIGKDD Innovation Award

One SIGKDD Innovation Award will be given to one individual or
one group of collaborators who has made significant technical
innovations in the field of Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery that
have been transferred to practice in significant ways, or that have
significantly influenced direction of research and development in the
field.

Previous SIGKDD Innovation Award winners were Rakesh Agrawal (IBM) in 2000 and 
Jerome Friedman 
(Stanford) in 2002.

SIGKDD Service Award

One SIGKDD Service Award will be given to one individual or one
group who has performed significant service to the field, that include
professional volunteer services in disseminating technical information
to the field, education, research funding, etc.

Previous SIGKDD Services Award winners were Gregory Piatetsky-Shapiro 
(KDnuggets) in 2000, and 
Ramasamy (Sam) Uthurusamy (GM) in 2002.

Nomination Process

Each nomination should be co-sponsored by at least 3 people.  Email
co-sponsorship is accepted.  Nominations should include a 200-500 word
statement to justify the nomination, and other supporting materials.

At most one award will be given each year in each category.

Please send all materials by email by June 8, 2002 to Gregory 
Piatetsky-Shapiro, 
gps at kdnuggets.com.

Important dates: 
1. Deadline for nominations: June 8, 2003.
2. Announcement of the Awards at ACM SIGKDD-2003 conference: August 24, 2003.

Exclusion:  People on the ACM SIGKDD Awards Committee (below) or SIGKDD Chairman
Won Kim are not eligible to be nominated.

ACM SIGKDD Awards Committee

Gregory Piatetsky-Shapiro (KDnuggets), Chair
Rakesh Agrawal (IBM)
Thomas Dietterich  (Oregon State University)

messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus users,
I have got some problems about input parameters for a Splus personal
procedure.

If I call the procedure below reported 
myprocedure(-38.94376,0.001842975)
there is an error in "smallg(Y1)" which says: 
Error in small(Y1): Object "E7" not found.
Why? 
E7 and V7 are two scalars.
Defining E7 and V7 as 
array(NA, dim = c(1, 1)),
mode(E7) is "numeric", mode(V7) is "numeric". 
I encounter the same problem if I define E7 and V7 as matrices of dimesion 1
by 1 
or even if I do not define them at all.
Why smallg can't be evaluated for eta=E7?
If I use the internal procedure without E7 and V7 but with pure numbers, i.e.

internal(-38.94376,0.001842975,1)
everything works fine. Why?

I am using Splus4 with W XP.

grateful for your help
Stefano

function(firstvalue, secondvalue)
{
E7 <- array(NA, dim = c(1, 1))
V7 <- array(NA, dim = c(1, 1))
E7 <- firstvalue
V7 <- secondvalue
internal <- function(normalmean, normalvariance, state){
alpha <- 0.01
if(state == 0) {
smallg <- substitute(function(eta){
(dnorm(eta, mean = normalmean, sd = sqrt(normalvariance)) * 1)/(1 + exp(alpha
* eta))})}
else {
smallg <- substitute(function(eta){
(dnorm(eta, mean = normalmean, sd = sqrt(normalvariance)) * exp(alpha *
eta))/(1 + exp(alpha * eta))})}
repeat {
# STEP 1: SAMPLE A POINT Y1 FROM bigg(Y)
Y1 <- rnorm(1, mean = normalmean, sd = sqrt(normalvariance)) 
# STEP 2: SAMPLE A UNIFORM(0,1) RANDOM VARIABLE U
U <- runif(1, min = 0, max = 1) 
# STEP 3: IF U <= g(Y1)/G(Y1) ACCEPT Y1; 
# REPEAT THIS LOOP UNTIL ONE Y IS ACCEPTED
if(U <= smallg(Y1)/dnorm(Y1, mean = normalmean, sd = sqrt(normalvariance))) {
sampledvalue <- Y1
break}}
result <- sampledvalue
result
}
finalvalue <- internal(E7, V7, 1)
}

messages.body_plain:
Stefano Sofia wrote:
> Dear Splus users,
> I have got some problems about input parameters for a Splus personal
> procedure.
>
> If I call the procedure below reported
> myprocedure(-38.94376,0.001842975)
>
> there is an error in "smallg(Y1)" which says:
> Error in small(Y1): Object "E7" not found.
>
> Why?
> E7 and V7 are two scalars.
>
> Defining E7 and V7 as
> array(NA, dim = c(1, 1)),
>
> mode(E7) is "numeric", mode(V7) is "numeric".
> I encounter the same problem if I define E7 and V7 as matrices of dimesion 1
>
> by 1
> or even if I do not define them at all.
>
> Why smallg can't be evaluated for eta=E7?
>
> If I use the internal procedure without E7 and V7 but with pure numbers, i.e.
>
>
>
> internal(-38.94376,0.001842975,1)
> everything works fine. Why?
>
> I am using Splus4 with W XP.
>
>
>
> grateful for your help
> Stefano

This is a scoping issue. Replace function internal with:

  internal <- function(normalmean, normalvariance, state){

    alpha <- 0.01

    if(state == 0) {

      smallg <- substitute(function(eta, mu, sigma){

        (dnorm(eta, mean = mu, sd = sigma) * 1)/(1 + exp(alpha * eta))})

    } else {

      smallg <- substitute(function(eta, mu, sigma){

        (dnorm(eta, mean = mu, sd = sigma) * exp(alpha * eta))/(1 + 
exp(alpha * eta))})

    }

    repeat {

      # STEP 1: SAMPLE A POINT Y1 FROM bigg(Y)

      Y1 <- rnorm(1, mean = normalmean, sd = sqrt(normalvariance))

      # STEP 2: SAMPLE A UNIFORM(0,1) RANDOM VARIABLE U

      U <- runif(1, min = 0, max = 1)

      # STEP 3: IF U <= g(Y1)/G(Y1) ACCEPT Y1;

      # REPEAT THIS LOOP UNTIL ONE Y IS ACCEPTED

      Y1.num <- smallg(Y1, normalmean, sqrt(normalvariance))

      Y1.den <- dnorm(Y1, mean = normalmean, sd = sqrt(normalvariance))

      if(U <= Y1.num/Y1.den) {

        sampledvalue <- Y1

        break

      }

    }

    result <- sampledvalue

    result

  }

Greetings,

I would like to implement a "flexible beta" heirarchical agglomerative
clustering method in Splus (version 6.0 running Windows 98).  Two versions
have been proposed: a weighted averages method (Lance and Williams 1967
[this has been implemented in SAS Proc Cluster]), and an unweighted/group
average method (Belbin et al. 1992).  I am most interested in the latter
group average method (also called UPGMA).  Has S code been written to
implement these clustering methods, and is such code available?

Thanks!

Erik Silldorff
Department of Ecology, Evolution, and Marine Biology
University of California, Santa Barbara

*************************
Lance, G.N. and W.T. Williams.  1966.  A general theory of classificatory
sorting strategies: I. Hierarchical systems.  Computer Journal 9: 373-380.

Belbin, L., D.P. Faith, and G.W. Milligan.  1992.  A comparison of two
approaches to beta-flexible clustering.  Multivariate Behavioral Research
27(3): 417-433.
*************************

messages.body_plain:
Hi all.

I have a nagging and somewhat transient problem.

I have a library, which contains a .First.lib.  In it, three files are
sourced:
source("my_functions.ssc", local = F, echo = F, n = -1, immediate = NULL)
source("my_callbacks.ssc", local = F, echo = F, n = -1, immediate = NULL)
source("add.my.menus.ssc", local = F, echo = F, n = -1, immediate = NULL)

The process works FOR THE MOST part: 99% of the functions in my_functions
are defined successfully and all the menus and 99% of the dialogs produced
by add.my.menus are OK.
Occasionally, something like this will happen upon loading the libraries:
*       a dialog will miss something like a text field; or
*       an occasional function will not be defined, so when you try to
invoke it from a dialog, SPLUS will complain.

It is all curable, if you run my_functions, my_callbacks and add.my.menus
MANUALLY, in which case no problem ever occurs.
I know there is a timing issue with sourcing files in that no assignments
are committed until "source" exits normally (though not sure what it would
explain). Is there any wisdom out there on how to get around this?

I use SPLUS 6.1Release 2 on Win 2000.

messages.body_plain:
"Tan Chuen Seng" <cmetcs at nus.edu.sg> asked
> The program repeatedly does a cox proportional hazard regression to the
> data, dat.ma, where the observations are in the rows and the different
> scenario in the columns. It works fine as a plain program but when I
> start to use the syntax function, it was unable to recognize the index
> 'w' in the for-loop (in S-Plus output: Object "w" not found).

This problem is a consequence of the approach taken to finding the data
in many S-Plus modeling functions.  (I am writing generalities now, 
because I haven't looked at the specifics of this function and version.)
Your function passes coxph() a formula argument

        Surv(dat.ma[,1],dat.ma[,2]) ~ dat.ma[,(w+2)]

The object dat.ma is probably being found not because it is the data argument
to the function, but rather because you are using the same name for an
object that is in an attached data directory.  You would get badly bitten
if you called rep.cox() with a different argument.  However, the object w 
containing the index lives in the frame of the function rep.cox, which is
not in the default search path for coxph when the latter is called.

Sometimes people handle this problem by assigning the object to the data
directory from the calling function using
assign("dataframename",computed.data.frame,wh=1).  In your case since the
form of the object is pretty simple, you can do it more neatly with something
like the following:

for(w in 1:no.obs) {
   sur.tmp <- coxph(Surv(a,b) ~ d,
        data=list(a=dat.ma[[1]],b=dat.ma[[2]],d=dat.ma[[w+2]]), 
        method='breslow')
    .... etc. ....
   }

messages.subject: Re: lme question
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

Here is a method to specify the var-cov matrix of the random effects
(suggested to me by Jose Pinheiro a while back):

##var-cov matrix for rand intercept and one rand slope
myfixedcov<-matrix(c(.09,-.01,-.01,.0075),2,2)

##Estimate the model specifying the form of the var-cov in pdSymm, and
##but not iterating, but only returning estimates that coincide with
#my choice of cov matrix.

themodel<-lme(Y~X+Z, data=thedata,
               random=list(group = pdSymm(myfixedcov,form=~X)),
               control=list(msMaxIter=0,niterEM=0))

##Check to see how close the resulting cov matrix is to myfixedcov.

(themodel$sigma^2) * pdMatrix(themodel$modelStruct$reStruct[[1]])

##Probably not exactly the same so:
##Repeat the estimation process, each time reweighting the cov matrix
##of random effects by sigma^2.

niter<-10
for(i in 1:10){
    themodel<-update(themodel,
                    random=list(CD=pdSymm(myfixedcov/themodel$sigma^2,
                                  form=~X)))
  }

##Check again: Probably much closer.
(themodel$sigma^2) * pdMatrix(themodel$modelStruct$reStruct[[1]])

You could add some kind of convergence criterion inside the loop so
that you don't have to choose a specific number of iterations.

I hope this helps.

Best,

Jake

-----

Jake Bowers
Dept of Political Science
University of Michigan

Dear Colleague:

 

I am using 
S+2000 (windows) and would like to 
know how to use COX 
model coefficients and 
statistics, without the original data set to estimate 
the baseline survival 
for a set of predictors including time-dependent covariates. 

 

The problem is that I don't have my raw 
dataset in S+ 
format, although I do 
have  the model coefficients as well as related model fit statistics generated from SAS. I was advised by 
S-plus support group that a COXPH OBJECT could do this job but needs some sophisticated programming using 
COEFFICIENTS, VAR, NAIVE.VAR, LOGLIK, SCORE, RSCORE, WALD.TEST, ITER, etc.  Converting the original dataset from SAS to S+ 
is not possible.  

 

I would highly appreciate it if someone can give 
me some help  on how to use this very useful 
tool only knowing the model statistics and not having the original 
dataset.

 

Thank you very much in advance! 

 

Jiahong

messages.subject: Seasonal decomposition of a time series with a few missing values
messages.subject_clean: Seasonal decomposition of a time series with a few missing values
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus 
listers,

I would like to use 
the stl() function (Seasonal-Trend Decomposition using Loess) on long term 
environmental data. I have monthly time series over 25-30 years, with a few 
values missing because of equipment failure or accidental loss of the data. 

The S-Plus 6.1 
implementation of the stl() function will not accept a time series with 
NAs. I was told by Insightful tech support that currently there is 
no way to set up stl() so that it will "smooth" over the missing 
values. I thought this would not be unreasonable since stl is using a 
sequence of loess smoothings.

Using the 
na.omit function to remove the NA 
values from the time series is not a valid 
solution because stl() does a 
seasonal decomposition of the time series and periodic position in the time 
series is very important. For instance 
if the value for the month of 
March 1983 is missing, na.omit removes it and then shortens 
the time series so the value for April 1983 becomes that of March 1983, and so 
forth.

I was told that 
a suitable work around 
(if there is not too many 
missing values) would be to just 
replace the NA's with a large number. Since stl() is robust, it will ignore these values in 
the algorithm, and essentially treat them as missing. What do you think of this solution? Do any of you have 
a better idea?

Cheers,

 

Marc 
Vayssières

 

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Marc Vayssières, Ph.D.

Environmental Scientist

California Department of Water 
Resources

3251 S Street

Sacramento, CA. 95816

(916) 227-7558

marcv at water.ca.gov
